opus-5.5.text:
I think the first thing I'd say is that there isn't one template that every country should copy. The UK institute was set up in a particular moment, with a particular level of political attention and funding, and with a lot of people coming in from the frontier labs and from academia. Not every country is going to have that, and they shouldn't feel they need to replicate it exactly.

What I'd encourage is for a country to ask: what is our comparative advantage, and where can we actually add something to the global picture? If you're a country that hosts frontier developers, then you have a special responsibility and a special opportunity. You can get close access to models, do pre-deployment testing, and build real technical depth on evaluations for things like cyber, chemical and biological misuse, and loss of control. If you're not hosting frontier labs, you can still do a lot of valuable work. You might focus on a particular research area where you have strong academic talent, or on the questions that matter most for how AI gets deployed in your own context. You might also put more weight on being a good partner in an international network: sharing methods, co-running evaluations, and helping develop the science of what we actually measure and why.

The second thing is that technical talent really matters. A safety institute that is mostly a policy shop, without people who can actually run and interpret evaluations, or do research on things like alignment and control, is going to struggle to be taken seriously by the labs and to give good advice to its own government. So the hiring model matters a lot. You need to be able to pay competitively, at least within the constraints of government, move quickly, and give technical people real autonomy. Being somewhat startup-like inside government was important for us.

Third, I'd say be honest about uncertainty. The science of evaluations is still immature. We don't have great ways to bound the risks of these systems, especially as they get more capable. An institute's job is partly to say what we know, but also to be clear about what we don't know and to fund and do the research that closes those gaps. That includes the harder, longer-term problems. If we only build evaluations for today's risks and don't invest in the theory and methods for showing that much more capable systems are safe, we'll be badly placed later.

Finally, I'd encourage countries to think of this as a collaborative enterprise rather than a competition. The problems are shared. If one institute develops a good evaluation methodology or finds an important result about how models can be misaligned, that's valuable to everyone. So build relationships early, with other institutes, with academia, and with the developers, and be willing to share.

r001.rationale: It recommends doing and funding research to close evaluation gaps, including longer-term problems, as a way to build technical depth.

r002.rationale: It encourages countries to focus on comparative advantages and collaborate, but does not clearly recommend avoiding attempts to evaluate the full range of AI risks individually.

r003.rationale: It recommends sharing methods and co-running evaluations with other institutes, but does not state that integrating evidence from institutes and nonprofits across governments helps governments acquire knowledge faster.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think the first thing I'd say is that it's quite dependent on the country. The UK and the US ended up in somewhat different places, and that's partly because of the different situations they were in. The UK doesn't host the frontier labs, so there's a natural question of what the UK's lever is, and the answer the UK AI Safety Institute landed on was: be very good at the technical work, build a serious evaluations capability, and then use that to be a credible voice internationally and to have real relationships with the labs. The US is in a different position because the labs are there, so there's more of a regulatory or quasi-regulatory flavour to what an institute there might do, even if it isn't formally a regulator.

So I think the first question a country should ask is: what is the comparative advantage here? What can we actually do that would matter? And I think for most countries the honest answer isn't "replicate everything the UK or US are doing." There are a few things that I think are genuinely valuable almost everywhere. One is having people in government who deeply understand the technology, because otherwise you're going to be making policy in a vacuum, and you'll be reliant on either the companies or on second-hand information. Building that technical capacity is just useful regardless of what else you do.

The second thing is that evaluations are a place where more effort is still helpful, but you have to be strategic about it. The frontier of evaluations in some areas — say, dangerous capabilities in bio or cyber — is already being worked on by a few institutes, and there's a question of whether you add value by doing the same thing, or whether you pick an area that's underserved. There are a lot of underserved areas. Societal impacts, specific languages and cultural contexts, specific domains where that country has expertise. If you're a country with a strong biosecurity community, lean into that. If you have a strong national security apparatus with particular knowledge, lean into that.

The third thing I'd emphasise is talent. The institutes that have worked have worked because they managed to hire people who could have been at the labs, and they got them to come work on this instead. That's hard inside a normal government structure. The UK had to do quite a lot of structural work to be able to pay people something approaching competitive salaries and to move quickly. If you set up an institute and then it's constrained by standard civil service hiring, I think it's going to struggle to be technically credible, and technical credibility is kind of the whole game. The labs will talk to you seriously if you can engage seriously with their work, and they won't if you can't.

And then the last thing is coordination. There's now an international network of these institutes, and I think a new one should think of itself as a node in that network rather than a standalone thing. Share evaluations, share methodology, don't duplicate effort unnecessarily, and figure out what you specifically can contribute. The risk of lots of institutes all doing the same thing in slightly different ways is real, and the upside of having many institutes each covering a different piece is quite large. So I'd say: start from your actual advantages, invest hard in technical talent, pick underserved problems, and plug into the network rather than trying to recreate the whole thing from scratch.

r001.rationale: The response recommends building technical capacity and evaluation capability, but does not identify conducting the institute’s own research as a way to do so.

r002.rationale: It recommends choosing underserved areas, sharing evaluations, and avoiding unnecessary duplication instead of trying to reproduce everything other institutes do.

r003.rationale: It recommends coordination and sharing evaluations and methods among institutes, but does not mention nonprofits or say that combining evidence helps governments acquire knowledge faster.

astra-6.text:
I think the first question is what role an institute can usefully play. You want technical expertise inside government, so that governments can assess what these systems can do, understand the risks, and make informed decisions. But that doesn’t mean every country needs to build an identical organisation with the same research agenda.

There’s a lot of value in specialisation. An institute could develop particular expertise in one kind of evaluation, or in the risks that matter most in its national context, and share that work with others. The important thing is that the institutes can collaborate: compare methods, share findings where appropriate, and build on each other’s work.

So I’d start with a clear technical mission and a strong team, and make international cooperation part of the design from the beginning. The goal should be to improve our collective ability to understand and manage the risks, rather than simply to have an institute in every country.

r001.rationale: The response recommends technical expertise and a strong team, but does not clearly say institutes should conduct their own research to build that capacity.

r002.rationale: It recommends specialisation in particular evaluations or nationally relevant risks, rather than each institute pursuing the same broad agenda, communicating that institutes should not individually cover the full range.

r003.rationale: It recommends collaboration and sharing findings, but does not mention nonprofits or say that integrating evidence helps governments acquire knowledge faster.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the first question is what role an institute can usefully play in that country. I wouldn’t assume that every country needs to reproduce the same organisation, with the same research agenda. There’s a lot of work to do, and there’s a real opportunity to specialise and share the results.

One useful distinction is between building technical expertise inside government and trying to do all the technical work yourself. Governments need enough expertise to understand what the risks are, assess the evidence, and ask good questions of companies. But that can involve collaborations with academics, other institutes, and independent researchers.

And I’d want these institutes to be able to work together internationally. If we’re evaluating the same models, we should be sharing methods and, where possible, findings, rather than each starting from scratch. That doesn’t mean countries have to agree on every policy question. It means developing a shared technical understanding that helps them make those decisions.

r001.rationale: The response calls for building technical expertise inside government and collaborating with outside researchers, but does not identify conducting the institutes’ own research as a way to build that capacity.

r002.rationale: It recommends specialisation and sharing results, but does not clearly say institutes should avoid individually evaluating the full range of AI risks.

r003.rationale: It supports international sharing of methods and findings, but does not mention integrating evidence from nonprofits or say that doing so helps governments acquire knowledge faster.
